articles.title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights
articles.summary: Existing laws are not equipped to address the risks to human rights being posed by artificial intelligence, UK politicians say.
articles.content:
A cross-party group of MPs and peers has identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI), arguing existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.

The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

"Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," said Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel.

Labour education minister Georgia Gould said AI was creating opportunities but that is was critical the government was "responding to those risks" posed by the technology.

In a summary of its 100-page report, the JCHR argued AI has been responsible for numerous abuses of human rights, citing examples including the use of AI to create sexualised images of women and girls, and scanning people's faces without their consent.

The JCHR has advocated for the creation of a "single, independent AI oversight body... on a statutory basis", saying the current legal framework is "fragmented and difficult to navigate", "leaving gaps in protection".

The report goes on to call for "more demanding obligations for higher risk AI systems and models" at all stages of the "AI lifecycle".

It continues: "Some uses of AI should be prohibited outright because they are incompatible with human rights. Potential areas for action include subliminal techniques, and inappropriate use of profiling or biometric data."

The committee's chair said: "AI is heralded as an unprecedented era of technological development with the potential to transform our lives for better or for worse."

"It is moving with such speed and complexity that its impact is hard to accurately predict. What is clear is that at present we are unprepared to deal with its consequences however potentially dire they may be."

The JCHR's 12 members are drawn from both Houses of Parliament and they currently include MPs and peers from the Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties.

Monday's report comes amid growing general anxiety over the challenges AI poses.

Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who quit Anthropic, told the BBC this weekend that staff developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.

An Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News that it was building "models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry".

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto said it would "ensure the safe development and use of AI models by introducing binding regulation on the handful of companies developing the most powerful AI models".

The government used the King's Speech in July 2024 to commit to bringing forward "appropriate legislation" but no dedicated AI bill appeared in this year's King's Speech.

Asked what has happened to the law promised by Labour, Gould told BBC Breakfast that the government "has been regulating" - including action to tackle non-consensual sexualised deepfakes and a bill linked to cyber security.

She said: "There is action happening and we're continuing to really carefully monitor the rise of AI, the way the technology is evolving and making sure we're staying alongside it and we have some of the best people in the world doing that work."

Gould said the AI Security Institute is "working through challenges coming in the future, testing models when they're coming into the UK", adding there is a need to work with other countries on the issue.

Following his arrival in No 10 in July, Prime Minister Andy Burnham ensured AI Minister Kanishka Narayan would attend cabinet meetings after scrapping the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and splitting its responsibilities among other government departments.

On Saturday, the head of the US AI company Anthropic, Dario Amodei, proposed a plan calling for the regulation of AI.

Amodei's plan includes global regulation, industry-wide regulation and independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed.

He also urged the pace of development to be slowed down and the bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, said they agreed with him.

One human rights concern raised in recent years is that AI can display biases against particular groups if trained on large datasets scraped from the internet which can include racist, sexist and other undesirable material.

AI could also be used to create and spread misinformation.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and positive development where UK lawmakers are proactively addressing the serious human rights risks posed by AI through calls for new legislation and oversight. This has broad societal impact as it aims to protect individuals from abuses such as non-consensual biometric surveillance and harmful profiling. The report is detailed and focused on establishing a regulatory framework to safeguard human rights in the face of rapidly advancing AI technology, which is a meaningful and inspiring step toward responsible AI governance.
articles.personality_title: UK lawmakers call for new AI law to protect human rights
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Artificial intelligence (AI) is growing quickly and affecting many parts of life. However, current laws in the UK are not strong enough to protect people's rights from new risks that AI can cause.

**What happened** – A group of UK politicians from different parties, called the Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR), released a report asking for a new law to better control AI. They want a law that can handle serious problems like AI making harmful images without permission or scanning faces without consent. The committee also suggests creating an independent organization to oversee AI and making stricter rules for risky AI systems.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows UK leaders are taking the dangers of AI seriously and want to protect people from misuse. By focusing on human rights, the report highlights real problems like privacy invasion and unfair treatment caused by AI. It also points out that some AI uses should be banned entirely if they harm people's rights.

**What's next step** – The UK government will need to consider this report and possibly create new laws and organizations to regulate AI better. They are already working on some related rules and plans, but this report pushes for a clearer, stronger approach. Cooperation with other countries is also expected since AI is a global issue.

**One-sentence takeaway** – UK politicians are pushing for new laws and oversight to protect human rights from the growing risks of artificial intelligence.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les législateurs britanniques réclament une nouvelle loi sur l’IA pour protéger les droits humains
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’intelligence artificielle (IA) se développe rapidement et touche de nombreux aspects de la vie. Cependant, les lois actuelles au Royaume-Uni ne sont pas assez fortes pour protéger les droits des personnes contre les nouveaux risques liés à l’IA.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un groupe de politiciens britanniques de différents partis, appelé le Comité mixte sur les droits de l’homme (JCHR), a publié un rapport demandant une nouvelle loi pour mieux contrôler l’IA. Ils souhaitent une loi capable de gérer des problèmes sérieux comme la création d’images nuisibles sans consentement ou la reconnaissance faciale non autorisée. Le comité propose aussi de créer une organisation indépendante pour superviser l’IA et d’imposer des règles plus strictes aux systèmes d’IA à haut risque.

**Impact** – C’est important car cela montre que les dirigeants britanniques prennent au sérieux les dangers de l’IA et veulent protéger les personnes contre les abus. En mettant l’accent sur les droits humains, le rapport souligne des problèmes concrets comme l’atteinte à la vie privée et les traitements injustes causés par l’IA. Il indique aussi que certains usages de l’IA devraient être interdits s’ils portent atteinte aux droits des individus.

**Prochaines étapes** – Le gouvernement du Royaume-Uni devra étudier ce rapport et peut-être créer de nouvelles lois et structures pour mieux réguler l’IA. Il travaille déjà sur certaines règles, mais ce rapport demande une approche plus claire et plus forte. Une coopération avec d’autres pays est aussi attendue, car l’IA est un enjeu mondial.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les politiciens britanniques réclament de nouvelles lois et une supervision pour protéger les droits humains face aux risques croissants de l’intelligence artificielle.

articles.title: Who is responsible for protecting and preserving Indigenous cultures?
articles.summary: As I read through the pieces Global Voices’ authors contributed to the August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights,” one common question stands out for me: Who gets to decide?
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.

There are 476 million Indigenous people in the world, about 6.2 percent of the global population. Though only 25 percent of the Earth’s landmass is left to be stewarded by these original inhabitants, they have long protected global biodiversity — often better than any official government programs and efforts. For hundreds of years, Indigenous groups have weathered colonization, violent settler occupation, oppression, and forced assimilation. Yet despite this dark past — which continues today in the 21st century — Indigenous people continue to fight for their fundamental rights and their own lands and resources.

As I read through the pieces Global Voices’ authors contributed to the August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights,” one common question stands out for me: Who gets to decide? We are past the question of whether Indigenous peoples deserve recognition, land, cultural, and political representation. The key is to ask who holds the power to grant or withhold, and who gets to decide on Indigenous identity, land, culture, safety, and profit.

Not all Indigenous peoples can claim their Indigenous identities because the state sometimes denies this right.

A genocide by the Ottoman Empire wiped out nearly 75 percent of the Assyrian people, and the Iraqi army led another genocide in 1933. Yet, not a single constitution of the region recognizes the Assyrians as an Indigenous people.

It took 30 years for Taiwan’s Siraya people to be officially recognized as Indigenous, but Japan’s Ryūkyūan people have only seen denials by the state. The Ryūkyūan were once removed from their own lands by the U.S. military during World War II. Decades later, the U.S. military continues to hoard Okinawan land through its military bases and destroy natural resources through unchecked pollution.

In Europe, “autochthonous,” perceived descendants of the original inhabitants, has become a discursive tool to promote nationalism and build hate against the “guests,” the immigrants. Ironically, depictions of Native American “heroes” in European popular culture have fuelled this.

While recognition as an Indigenous people is a critical first step for any Indigenous community, it does not always translate to decision-making. When Indigenous leaders in Nueva Vizcaya, the Philippines, organized an anti-mining rally, they were arrested and charged, with over 30 criminal cases filed against them. Brazil’s case was even scarier — 258 Indigenous people were murdered in 2025 for defending their land rights, according to Cimi (the Missionary Indigenist Council). In Thailand, mining activities are polluting the Kok River. Hundreds of villagers, Indigenous leaders, monks, and civil and environmental rights activists carried out a “peace walk” to defend their Indigenous cultural identity and a vital source of drinking water, irrigation, fisheries, and transportation.

Almost always, when the state goes against its Indigenous peoples, it is to extract the latter’s lands, waters, other natural resources, or community products. Lack of Indigenous recognition also translates to significant state control over lands and land-related decisions. China’s new cotton law mechanized cotton production, making the cotton supply chain state-traceable, state-inspectable, and state-governable through data. Concurrently, this policy coerced over seven million Uyghur, Tibetan, and other Indigenous farmers to use their own lands under significant government supervision. In northern Tanzania, the Indigenous Maasai lands are taken by the state in the name of environmental protection only to use them for tourism, hunting, and private investments.

All of these stories raise the original question — who gets to decide. When Indigenous communities control decisions, they are able to protect and nurture their lands, resources, languages, and cultures. For example, 14 members of the Kam community in Nigeria created 307 audiovisual recordings in the Kam language, which has 8,000–11,000 speakers, after receiving training from a linguist, buffering against the threat of language endangerment. In India, Kshetrabasi Juanga, an Indigenous educator, goes from village to village, documenting the endangered Juang language. Far away in Russia, the Buryat fashion designer Oksana Alkhunsaeva has created an occupation for herself that both employs and supports her whole family, and keeps the Buryat textile heritage alive.

The question of who gets to decide also shapes the impact of modernization on Indigenous communities. As Nepal’s Rana Tharu language is threatened due to the prioritization of English and Nepali, women often become the last line of defense, preventing the loss of local languages. Dambe, a martial art form of Nigeria’s Hausa tribe, sees the new safety measures, regulations, and modernization through organized tournaments as a welcome step. But YouTube contests that attract external participation and viewership are erasing the Hausa cultural heritage long associated with it.

There is a strong case for the protection of Indigenous knowledge, and even state support, when its economic value flows into the community. Ghana’s traditional medicine sector serves 60 to 70 percent of the population, as the profit-driven Western medicine market fails to make medicines affordable. The cassava, millet, and sorghum market is expanding across Africa, as these Indigenous crops are a better alternative to imported wheat- economical and gluten-free- opening potential for leading an international market. Indigenous knowledge and data are a core part of AI policies. As Chadian environmental activist Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim rightly puts it, “Indigenous peoples must be recognized as rights holders and decision-makers — especially when newfangled technology has implications for their lands or intellectual heritage.”

The state’s control over Indigenous bodies goes hand-in-hand with state surveillance. In Australia, Indigenous children are 23 times more likely to be under supervision and 28 times more likely to be in detention.

What really stands out for me is what Genner Llanes-Ortiz, a Mexican Mayan researcher, argues — most modern state structures have categorically failed to understand the Indigenous communities. These societies once lived on the lands that provide homes to the descendants of settler-colonists as well as those who arrived in other ways.

One important human aspect we may forget when discussing these issues is that the onus of protecting and preserving Indigenous cultures falls on individuals like Kshetrabasi Juang or Oksana Alkhunsaeva. There is an urgent need for resources — for more Indigenous individuals to collaborate before the few individual leaders burn out.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the ongoing struggles and resilience of Indigenous peoples worldwide in protecting their cultures, lands, and rights. It emphasizes the importance of Indigenous decision-making power and showcases concrete examples of cultural preservation and activism, which have broad societal significance and inspire hope for Indigenous empowerment and cultural survival.
articles.personality_title: Who decides the future of Indigenous cultures and lands?
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Indigenous peoples are the original inhabitants of many lands around the world. There are about 476 million Indigenous people, making up 6.2% of the global population. Despite facing colonization, violence, and discrimination for hundreds of years, they continue to protect their lands, cultures, and rights.

**What happened**
A recent series called “Indigenous Rights” by Global Voices highlights stories from Indigenous communities worldwide. It asks an important question: Who has the power to decide about Indigenous identity, land, culture, and safety? Many Indigenous groups still struggle to be officially recognized by their governments. Some face violence and legal challenges when they try to defend their lands. Yet, Indigenous people are also working to preserve their languages, traditions, and knowledge through education, art, and activism.

**Impact**
This series shows that recognition alone is not enough; Indigenous peoples need real decision-making power to protect their cultures and environments. For example, in Nigeria, the Kam community recorded their language to keep it alive. In India and Russia, Indigenous individuals are documenting languages and preserving traditional crafts. These actions help keep cultures strong even when outside forces threaten them. The stories also reveal how governments sometimes use Indigenous lands for their own benefit, ignoring Indigenous rights.

**What’s next step**
More support and resources are needed for Indigenous leaders and communities. This includes helping more people work together to protect languages, lands, and traditions before current leaders become overwhelmed. Recognizing Indigenous peoples as decision-makers in government policies, especially around natural resources and technology, will be crucial for their future.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Indigenous peoples’ power to decide about their cultures and lands is key to preserving their heritage and protecting the environment.
articles.personality_title_fr: Qui décide de l’avenir des cultures et des terres autochtones ?
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
Les peuples autochtones sont les habitants originels de nombreuses terres dans le monde. Ils sont environ 476 millions, soit 6,2 % de la population mondiale. Malgré des siècles de colonisation, de violence et de discrimination, ils continuent de protéger leurs terres, leurs cultures et leurs droits.

**Ce qui s’est passé**
Une série récente intitulée « Droits autochtones » de Global Voices met en lumière des histoires de communautés autochtones à travers le monde. Elle pose une question importante : qui a le pouvoir de décider de l’identité, des terres, de la culture et de la sécurité autochtones ? Beaucoup de groupes autochtones peinent encore à être officiellement reconnus par leurs gouvernements. Certains font face à la violence et à des poursuites quand ils défendent leurs terres. Pourtant, ils travaillent aussi à préserver leurs langues, traditions et savoirs grâce à l’éducation, l’art et l’activisme.

**Impact**
Cette série montre que la reconnaissance seule ne suffit pas ; les peuples autochtones doivent avoir un vrai pouvoir de décision pour protéger leurs cultures et leurs environnements. Par exemple, au Nigeria, la communauté Kam a enregistré sa langue pour la préserver. En Inde et en Russie, des individus autochtones documentent des langues et préservent des savoir-faire traditionnels. Ces actions aident à garder les cultures vivantes même face aux menaces extérieures. Les récits révèlent aussi comment certains gouvernements utilisent les terres autochtones à leur profit, sans respecter leurs droits.

**Prochaine étape**
Plus de soutien et de ressources sont nécessaires pour les leaders et communautés autochtones. Il faut aider davantage de personnes à collaborer pour protéger les langues, terres et traditions avant que les leaders actuels ne s’épuisent. Reconnaître les peuples autochtones comme décideurs dans les politiques gouvernementales, surtout sur les ressources naturelles et la technologie, sera essentiel pour leur avenir.

**Phrase clé**
Le pouvoir des peuples autochtones à décider de leurs cultures et terres est essentiel pour préserver leur héritage et protéger l’environnement.
articles.personality_title_es: ¿Quién decide el futuro de las culturas y tierras indígenas?
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
Los pueblos indígenas son los habitantes originales de muchas tierras en el mundo. Hay alrededor de 476 millones de indígenas, que representan el 6,2 % de la población mundial. A pesar de siglos de colonización, violencia y discriminación, continúan protegiendo sus tierras, culturas y derechos.

**Qué pasó**
Una serie reciente llamada «Derechos Indígenas» de Global Voices destaca historias de comunidades indígenas en todo el mundo. Plantea una pregunta importante: ¿quién tiene el poder de decidir sobre la identidad, las tierras, la cultura y la seguridad indígena? Muchos grupos indígenas aún luchan por ser reconocidos oficialmente por sus gobiernos. Algunos enfrentan violencia y problemas legales al defender sus tierras. Sin embargo, también trabajan para preservar sus idiomas, tradiciones y conocimientos mediante la educación, el arte y el activismo.

**Impacto**
Esta serie muestra que solo el reconocimiento no basta; los pueblos indígenas necesitan tener un poder real de decisión para proteger sus culturas y ambientes. Por ejemplo, en Nigeria, la comunidad Kam grabó su idioma para mantenerlo vivo. En India y Rusia, personas indígenas documentan idiomas y preservan artesanías tradicionales. Estas acciones ayudan a mantener las culturas fuertes incluso cuando fuerzas externas las amenazan. Las historias también revelan cómo a veces los gobiernos usan las tierras indígenas para su propio beneficio, ignorando sus derechos.

**Próximo paso**
Se necesitan más apoyos y recursos para los líderes y comunidades indígenas. Esto incluye ayudar a que más personas trabajen juntas para proteger idiomas, tierras y tradiciones antes de que los líderes actuales se agoten. Reconocer a los pueblos indígenas como tomadores de decisiones en las políticas gubernamentales, especialmente sobre recursos naturales y tecnología, será clave para su futuro.

**Frase clave**
El poder de los pueblos indígenas para decidir sobre sus culturas y tierras es clave para preservar su herencia y proteger el medio ambiente.

articles.title: What the commemoration of the 235th anniversary of Bois Caïman means for Haiti’s memory and future
articles.summary: August 14, 1791, put in motion the first major anti-slavery movement in Haiti — part Vodou ceremony, part political congress, and wholly a movement of protest and resistance.
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The night of August 14, 1791, marked the beginning of a series of events that changed the world. A large group of enslaved people and rebel leaders met at Bwa Kayiman (Bois Caïman), a historic site located in Haiti’s Northern Department, in the town of Plaine-du-Nord.

Under the leadership of the houngan (Vodou priest) Dutty Boukman and manbo (priestess) Cécile Fatiman — along with key resistance leaders — the gathering brought together enslaved people from different plantations for a clandestine religious and political ceremony. They invoked the lwa and ancestral spiritual forces, seeking their protection and strength for the struggle ahead.

It set in motion the first major anti-slavery movement in Saint-Domingue (which would later become Haiti), as enslaved people fought for their freedom. At that time, the island of Hispaniola was divided into two European colonies: the western part was the French colony of Saint-Domingue, and the eastern part was the Spanish colony of Santo Domingo; the modern republics did not yet exist.

During this time, Saint-Domingue was one of the world’s richest sugar and coffee colonies, built on an economy that depended entirely on the slave trade. To stop this terrible human suffering, enslaved people united to resist one of the most powerful colonial empires of the 18th century.

Coming together to resist

The resulting uprising brought together different groups of enslaved people. The population included Creole enslaved people who were born on the island, spoke Haitian Creole, understood French, and worked as skilled workers (carpenters, blacksmiths, masons, shoemakers, or house servants); “Bossales,” enslaved people who were brought directly from Africa on a négrier (slave ship), endured the hardest labour conditions and suffered brutal physical punishments, yet held onto their African roots, languages, songs, and Vodou traditions, and domestic or “elite” enslaved people who worked in the masters’ homes as servants, cooks, bodyguards, hairdressers, wet nurses, cochers (horse-drawn carriage drivers), or commandeurs (plantation slave leaders).

In this harsh environment, enslaved women often suffered sexual abuse from colonisers, which led to a mixed-race population, while plantation leaders were often forced to enforce rules with great severity. While the plantation owners tried to turn these groups against each other, the movement found strong support in les Nègres Marrons (the Maroons), who escaped the plantations and mines, and fled to the mountains to fight back.

Dehumanising treatment

During this period, plantation slaves made up the overwhelming majority of Saint-Domingue’s enslaved population, performing the most rigorous tasks and working relentless schedules from dawn until well into the night. When they arrived at colonial ports after weeks in the holds of slave ships travelling from Africa to the Americas, they were branded with heated irons as marks of identification and ownership. Branding also marked medical information or past flight attempts.

Enslaved people were routinely beaten with whips and straps made from dried cowhide, which tore through their skin and left large, bloody wounds. Other punishments included being chained in dark basements for several days, often without food. If someone rebelled, an overseer might force another enslaved person to cut off an ear, arm, or leg as a brutal deterrent to others on the plantation.

The most cruel punishments involved public hangings, beheadings, or torture. Recaptured fugitives faced these brutal penalties, and plantation mortality was high. When enslaved people grew too old or sick to perform hard labour, they were often abandoned and left to die, or executed by plantation owners who viewed them as burdens.

In stark contrast to domestic slaves and overseers, who had access to better food, agricultural and mine slaves survived mainly on water and cassava. This, coupled with the terrible labour conditions and widespread dehumanisation, ultimately fuelled the mass collective resistance that resulted in the Bois Caïman uprising.

From fight to freedom

From the mountains, these rebel fighters employed guerrilla tactics. Using weapons like slingshots, knives, machetes, and arrows, they ambushed and attacked colonial soldiers, took their weapons, poisoned water sources and animals, and burned plantations and their houses. Most of the time, these attacks took place at night, while the colonists were sleeping.

They also built a strong intelligence network. From house servants to drivers, enslaved people worked as spies to send information about hidden weapons to rebel commanders, using kònn lanbi (conch shells) and drums to send signals across the mountains. Vodou ceremonies helped prepare the fighters, who bathed in natural plant mixtures and used special powders for protection.

Following the Bois Caïman ceremony, the anti-slavery struggle continued over 12 years through the leadership of key figures such as Toussaint Louverture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Henri Christophe, Alexandre Pétion, François Capois, and Jean-Pierre Boyer. Women also played a central role in sustaining this revolution, including Marie-Jeanne Lamartinière, Sanité Bélair, Catherine Flon, and Claire Heureuse.

This movement ultimately led to the Battle of Vertières on November 18, 1803, where the insurgent army defeated the French colonial forces in the western part of Saint-Domingue. This victory brought an end to slavery in the former colony and resulted in the declaration of the first Black republic in the world — Haitian independence on January 1, 1804. Later, during the unification of the island under President Boyer in 1822, slavery was also formally abolished in the eastern Spanish-speaking side. (Under President Boyer, the Haitian government occupied the eastern part of the island, formerly Santo Domingo. This occupation began on February 9, 1822, and ended 22 years later on February 27, 1844, when the eastern side declared its independence from Haiti.)

Modern-day perspectives

To mark the 235th anniversary of this significant historic event at Bois Caïman, on August 14, 2026, various socio-cultural, Vodou, and conference/debate events were organised across the country, including an event in Cap-Haïtien organised by Kenbe Kapow, a collective founded in 2025 by a group of young people. According to Peterson Jules, Kenbe Kapow’s secretary general, who spoke with Global Voices via a WhatsApp call, it acts as an advocacy group to demand accountability from local authorities, raise civic awareness among citizens, and encourage political engagement.

In addition to political leaders, the event brought together public figures from academic, literary, and cultural sectors, and featured patriotic songs, dance performances, and discussions about the role of Bois Caïman in making Haiti the world’s first independent Black republic. Panellists also emphasised the need for national unity to address Haiti’s multi-dimensional challenges — particularly the ongoing political crisis, gang violence, and widespread public despair.

In comparing historical marronage to the country’s present-day challenges, Kenbe Kapow’s Communications Officer Karlin Georges Le Pont highlighted the importance of individual and collective responsibility:

Nou te genyen yon etap mawon, mawonaj kote esklav yo pou te ka soti sou difikilte dominasyon nan chan yo te pran chimen mòn, men yo pa t pran l pou yo te kapab deresponsabilize yo. Se te yon fòm rezistans ke moman an te mande, e pandan yo te nan mawon yo te reflechi sou kouman yo kapab pran libète yo. Si n ap eseye fè yon paralèl ak epòk sa yo, jodi a n ap viv nan yon epòk mawonaj kote ayisyen an mawon tèt li, ayisyen an mawon peyi l, ayisyen an mawon moun li ye a. Kontrèman ak ansyen mawon yo ki te mawon pou te kapab cherche libète, nou menm nou mawon paske nou di nou fatige, nou pap batay ankò. An nou soti nan etap mawonaj la pou nou vin nan etap kongrè a, etap ransebleman an ak tout fòs viv patriyòt nasyon an pou nou chita pou yon Ayiti miyò pou tout moun.

We had a stage of marronage where the enslaved, to escape the harsh domination in the fields, took to the mountains. However, they did not do so to shirk their responsibilities; it was a form of resistance required by that time. While in marronage, they reflected on how to achieve their freedom. Drawing a parallel to today, we are living in a time of modern marronage where Haitians are hiding from themselves, their country, and their identity. Unlike the former Maroons who fled to seek freedom, we flee because we say we are tired and will no longer fight. Let us move past this stage of marronage and enter the stage of the congress — a stage of gathering all the patriotic living forces of the nation to sit together for a better Haiti for everyone.

Politician and former senior state official Sterline Civil stressed the need for civic duty and action over rhetoric, noting that Haitians “must work to show that we are worthy” of the Bois Caïman heritage. “Otherwise,” she claimed, “we will never succeed and will only continue to make grand speeches.”

In a similar vein, architect and local leader Wideline Pierre emphasised the need for unity and shared purpose, suggesting that if Haitians want to emerge from the current social, political, and economic situation, they “must realise that unity, konbit (collective labor), and solidarity are what define us as a people.”

A new Bois Caïman?

Dominique Dupuy, a former minister and Haitian ambassador to UNESCO, suggested:

Se yon dezyèm Bwa Kayiman nou bezwen, se yon dezyèm chita nou bezwen, yon dezyèm gran ransebleman, yon dezyèm gwo konba nou bezwen. Se tout ayisyen nan tout orizon, patisipan yo, sa ki deyò yo, ak vwazinaj nou, zanmi nou, ak kominite nou ki ka leve jou an kò pou Ayiti, pou Ayiti zansèt yo te imajine a, pou Ayiti pitit nou yo merite a, pou yon Ayiti kote nou pap sèlman sibi jou après jou nan chèche lavi, men nan chèche lavi nou jwenn li pandan nou vivan.

We need a second Bwa Kayiman, a second sit-down meeting, a second great gathering, and a second major battle. It is all Haitians from all backgrounds, those present, those abroad, along with our neighbours, friends, and community, who can make the sun rise again for Haiti — for the Haiti our ancestors imagined, for the Haiti our children deserve, and for a Haiti where we do not merely survive day after day searching for life, but where we find life while we are alive.

Rekindling protest

On the actual historic site, the 235th anniversary commemoration involved houngans, manbos, and others from the Artibonite department — a region severely impacted by gang violence — gathering to honour their ancestors. Participants dressed in vibrant Afro-Caribbean attire adorned with vèvè symbols and portraits of lwas.

The atmosphere vibrated with the sounds of traditional instruments, including tanbou (drums), klòch (bells), and chachà (rattles). Spectators came in their numbers to the Bois Caïman grounds, where a stage and loudspeakers set the mood with traditional, rasin, and protest music.

There was a shared spirit of communion through song, dance, and protest. Marching across the site, participants carried banners bearing direct messages and demands: Ayiti pou Vodou, Vodou pou Ayiti (Haiti for Vodou, Vodou for Haiti); Aba Jezi kolon (Down with the colonial Jesus); Nou mande Leta bay peyi a sekirite (We demand that the government provide security for the country); Nou mande pou Leta retire 52/100 li bay legliz nan bidjè a (We demand that the state remove the 52 percent allocated to churches from the national budget); Jezi fè nou esklav, Desalin libere nou (Jesus made us slaves, Dessalines freed us); and Viv Ewò yo (Long live the Heroes).

Despite the historic epic achieved by Haiti’s founders who survived the transatlantic slave trade, defeated Napoleon Bonaparte’s army, and changed the course of history, the battle for true freedom is far from over.

Two hundred and twenty-two years after achieving independence, Haiti remains a unique symbol of human freedom. Yet, the nation still suffers from poverty, chronic political instability, systemic corruption, gang violence, and foreign interference.

Regardless, Haiti possesses the resources needed for its people to live with dignity as the ancestors intended, and the fight for full sovereignty, economic freedom, and social justice remains unfinished.

The greatest challenge for the Haitian people to emerge from this endemic crisis is the need for a new political and economic class, alongside a new model of civil society. This new generation of leaders must have a genuine commitment to Haiti, a clear vision, and the willingness to set personal interests aside to prioritize the nation's well-being.

articles.personality_title: Remembering Bois Caïman: Haiti’s 235th anniversary of freedom and resistance
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – On August 14, 1791, enslaved people in what is now Haiti gathered at Bois Caïman for a secret ceremony. This meeting started a major rebellion against slavery in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, which eventually led to Haiti’s independence and the end of slavery.

**What happened** – Led by Vodou priests Dutty Boukman and Cécile Fatiman, enslaved people from different plantations came together to plan a fight for freedom. They used traditional ceremonies to ask for spiritual strength and then began a 12-year struggle against French colonial forces. This fight ended with Haiti becoming the world’s first Black republic in 1804.

**Impact** – The Bois Caïman ceremony was the spark for a powerful movement that changed history. It united people from different backgrounds to resist cruelty and slavery. Today, Haitians remember this event to inspire political action, national unity, and hope despite ongoing challenges like violence and poverty.

**What’s next step** – In 2026, young groups and leaders held events to honor Bois Caïman’s legacy and called for a new spirit of cooperation and responsibility. They want Haitians to move beyond division and work together for a better future. This includes building new leaders committed to justice and progress.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The 235th anniversary of Bois Caïman reminds Haiti and the world that freedom began with unity and courage, and that the fight for a just society continues today.
articles.personality_title_fr: Commémorer Bois Caïman : 235 ans de liberté et de résistance en Haïti
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le 14 août 1791, des esclaves de ce qui est aujourd’hui Haïti se sont réunis secrètement à Bois Caïman. Cette rencontre a déclenché une grande rébellion contre l’esclavage dans la colonie française de Saint-Domingue, menant finalement à l’indépendance d’Haïti et à la fin de l’esclavage.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Sous la direction des prêtres vaudous Dutty Boukman et Cécile Fatiman, des esclaves de différentes plantations se sont unis pour préparer la lutte pour leur liberté. Ils ont utilisé des cérémonies traditionnelles pour demander la force spirituelle, puis ont mené une lutte de 12 ans contre les forces coloniales françaises. Cette lutte a abouti à la création de la première république noire au monde en 1804.

**Impact** – La cérémonie de Bois Caïman a été l’étincelle d’un mouvement puissant qui a changé l’histoire. Elle a uni des personnes de divers horizons pour résister à la cruauté et à l’esclavage. Aujourd’hui, les Haïtiens se souviennent de cet événement pour inspirer l’action politique, l’unité nationale et l’espoir malgré les défis actuels comme la violence et la pauvreté.

**Prochaine étape** – En 2026, des jeunes et des leaders ont organisé des événements pour honorer l’héritage de Bois Caïman et appeler à un nouvel esprit de coopération et de responsabilité. Ils souhaitent que les Haïtiens dépassent leurs divisions pour construire ensemble un avenir meilleur, avec de nouveaux dirigeants engagés pour la justice et le progrès.

**Phrase clé** – Le 235e anniversaire de Bois Caïman rappelle à Haïti et au monde que la liberté a commencé par l’unité et le courage, et que la lutte pour une société juste continue aujourd’hui.
articles.personality_title_es: Recordando Bois Caïman: 235 años de libertad y resistencia en Haití
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El 14 de agosto de 1791, esclavos en lo que hoy es Haití se reunieron en secreto en Bois Caïman. Esta reunión inició una gran rebelión contra la esclavitud en la colonia francesa de Saint-Domingue, que llevó a la independencia de Haití y al fin de la esclavitud.

**Qué pasó** – Liderados por los sacerdotes vudú Dutty Boukman y Cécile Fatiman, esclavos de diferentes plantaciones se unieron para planear la lucha por su libertad. Usaron ceremonias tradicionales para pedir fuerza espiritual y luego comenzaron una lucha de 12 años contra las fuerzas coloniales francesas. Esta lucha terminó con la creación de la primera república negra del mundo en 1804.

**Impacto** – La ceremonia de Bois Caïman fue la chispa de un poderoso movimiento que cambió la historia. Unió a personas de distintos orígenes para resistir la crueldad y la esclavitud. Hoy, los haitianos recuerdan este evento para inspirar acción política, unidad nacional y esperanza a pesar de los retos actuales como la violencia y la pobreza.

articles.title: Guterres: Old global order must change as power shifts to emerging economies
articles.summary: UN Secretary-General António Guterres told leaders of a bloc of major emerging economies in New Delhi on Sunday that a more balanced global order requires an overhaul of the institutions built after the Second World War, including the UN Security Council.
articles.content:
The group – Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and several other nations that have also signed on – was founded to give major developing economies a stronger voice in a global system long dominated by Western powers.

This year's summit, hosted by India, has drawn heads of state alongside the leaders of the World Health Organization and the World Trade Organization.

Tweet URL

Reflecting reality

“Today's economic, demographic and geopolitical realities are not those of 1945,” Mr. Guterres said. “Our institutional structures must reflect it.”

He told the assembled leaders that they themselves embodied the change he was describing. "Countries represented at this Summit speak to that changing reality," he said, adding that “we are increasingly moving towards a multipolar world.”

That shift, he argued, was something to embrace rather than resist. “Multipolarity helps bring balance and equity to global systems and institutions,” he said – but only if it comes with reform of bodies including the Security Council and the Bretton Woods system “to reflect the world of today.”

Go for growth

Mr. Guterres framed four priorities for what he called "inclusive global growth": financing, technology, climate justice and peace.

On finance, he said developing countries “need massive international support” to meet the Sustainable Development Goals, and called for multilateral development banks to become “bigger, better and bolder.”

On artificial intelligence, he warned the technology's benefits remained concentrated. “Its power sits with a few companies, in a few countries,” he said. “Unchecked, the AI divide will widen every other divide — in income, in opportunity, in security, and in sovereignty.”

Dangerous climate

His starkest language came on climate. “Scorching heat, devastating glacier melt, raging wildfires, devastating floods are all a preview,” he said, warning that “a supersized El Niño will only make matters worse” as the world approaches the 1.5-degree limit above pre-industrial levels.

He pressed wealthy nations to honour existing pledges – $300 billion dollars a year, tripled adaptation finance, and greater loss and damage funding – and took aim at the handling of critical minerals: “Enough plundering.”

On peace and security, he pointed to Gaza, the wider Middle East, Ukraine and Sudan, calling on states to uphold the UN Charter, including “sovereign equality,” territorial integrity and “peaceful settlement of disputes.”

Collective responsibility

He closed by casting the reform agenda as a shared project rather than a concession. “As we move irreversibly to a multipolar world, all countries must work to strengthen and safeguard a multilateral system that delivers for all with the United Nations at its centre,” he said.

articles.personality_title: UN chief calls for global system reform to match new world powers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The world’s global institutions, like the United Nations Security Council, were created after World War II. Since then, the balance of economic and political power has shifted, with emerging economies like India, Brazil, and China becoming much stronger.

**What happened** – On Sunday in New Delhi, UN Secretary-General António Guterres spoke to leaders from a group of major emerging economies. He said these institutions must change to better reflect today’s world. The meeting included countries like Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, as well as leaders from the World Health Organization and World Trade Organization.

**Impact** – Guterres said the world is moving toward a multipolar system, where power is shared more evenly among many countries, not just Western ones. He emphasized that this change can bring fairness but only if global institutions are updated. He also focused on four key areas: fair financing for developing countries, making technology like artificial intelligence more accessible, urgent action on climate change, and peace efforts in conflict zones.

**What's next step** – The leaders are expected to work on reforming global institutions and increasing support for development and climate action. This could lead to stronger cooperation between countries and more balanced decision-making on world issues.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN chief urges updating global institutions to better share power and address today’s economic, technological, and environmental challenges fairly and peacefully.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le chef de l’ONU appelle à réformer le système mondial pour refléter les nouvelles puissances
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les institutions mondiales comme le Conseil de sécurité de l’ONU ont été créées après la Seconde Guerre mondiale. Depuis, le poids économique et politique a changé, avec l’émergence de pays comme l’Inde, le Brésil et la Chine.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dimanche à New Delhi, le secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a parlé aux dirigeants d’un groupe de grandes économies émergentes. Il a déclaré que ces institutions doivent évoluer pour mieux refléter le monde actuel. Cette réunion regroupait des pays comme le Brésil, la Russie, l’Inde, la Chine et l’Afrique du Sud, ainsi que des responsables de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé et de l’Organisation mondiale du commerce.

**Impact** – Guterres a expliqué que le monde se dirige vers un système multipolaire, où le pouvoir est partagé entre plusieurs pays et pas seulement les pays occidentaux. Il a souligné que ce changement peut apporter plus d’équité, mais seulement si les institutions mondiales sont modernisées. Il a aussi mis l’accent sur quatre priorités : un financement juste pour les pays en développement, un accès plus large aux technologies comme l’intelligence artificielle, une action urgente contre le changement climatique, et des efforts pour la paix.

**Prochaine étape** – Les dirigeants devraient travailler à réformer les institutions mondiales et à renforcer le soutien au développement et à la lutte contre le climat. Cela pourrait renforcer la coopération entre pays et rendre les décisions mondiales plus équilibrées.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le chef de l’ONU appelle à moderniser les institutions mondiales pour mieux partager le pouvoir et relever équitablement et pacifiquement les défis économiques, technologiques et environnementaux d’aujourd’hui.
articles.personality_title_es: El jefe de la ONU pide reformar el sistema global para reflejar nuevas potencias
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las instituciones globales, como el Consejo de Seguridad de la ONU, se crearon después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Desde entonces, el equilibrio de poder económico y político ha cambiado, con economías emergentes como India, Brasil y China ganando fuerza.

**Qué pasó** – El domingo en Nueva Delhi, el Secretario General de la ONU, António Guterres, habló con líderes de un grupo de grandes economías emergentes. Dijo que estas instituciones deben cambiar para reflejar mejor el mundo actual. La reunión incluyó países como Brasil, Rusia, India, China y Sudáfrica, así como líderes de la Organización Mundial de la Salud y la Organización Mundial del Comercio.

**Impacto** – Guterres señaló que el mundo se mueve hacia un sistema multipolar, donde el poder se comparte más equitativamente entre muchos países, no solo los occidentales. Destacó que este cambio puede traer justicia, pero solo si se actualizan las instituciones globales. También se enfocó en cuatro áreas clave: financiamiento justo para países en desarrollo, acceso más equitativo a tecnologías como la inteligencia artificial, acción urgente contra el cambio climático y esfuerzos de paz.

**Próximo paso** – Se espera que los líderes trabajen en reformar las instituciones globales y aumenten el apoyo para el desarrollo y la acción climática. Esto podría llevar a una cooperación más fuerte entre países y decisiones más equilibradas sobre problemas mundiales.

**Frase clave** – El jefe de la ONU pide actualizar las instituciones globales para compartir mejor el poder y enfrentar de manera justa y pacífica los retos económicos, tecnológicos y ambientales actuales.
